titel: The super-logarithm counts exponentials: χ(f) = lim (slog f(x) − slog x)
aussage:
Set $\chi(f)=\lim_{x\to\infty}\bigl(A(f(x))-A(x)\bigr)$, where the limit exists. Then:
(i) $\chi(\exp)=1$, $\chi(\ln)=-1$, $\chi(f\circ g)=\chi(f)+\chi(g)$, and $\chi(\exp^{[s]})=s$ for $\exp^{[s]}(x)=T(A(x)+s)$ — a half-exponential function has $\chi=\tfrac12$.

(ii) $\chi(f)=0$ for $cx$, $x+c$, $x^k$, $x^{\ln x}$; $\chi(f)=1$ for $2^x$, $x^x$, $e^{x^2}$ — in general $\chi$ is, for every exp-log function and every transseries, an
integer, the exponentiality in the sense of Hardy and van der Hoeven.

(iii) An **integer** exponentiality is the same for every super-logarithm; a **fractional** one is not: with another $\tilde A=A+\theta(A)$ ($\theta$ 1-periodic) one has
$\tilde A(\exp^{[1/2]}x)-\tilde A(x)=\tfrac12+\theta(A(x)+\tfrac12)-\theta(A(x))$ — this oscillates if $\theta$ is not $\tfrac12$-periodic.

At $x=e\uparrow\uparrow k$, $k=2,\dots,5$: for $x^2$ the difference is $0.529$, $0.197$, $0.0149$, $4.0\cdot10^{-9}$.
bereich: increasing $f$ with $f(x)\to\infty$; $A=\operatorname{slog}_e$ continuous, strictly increasing, with $A(y+c)-A(y)\to0$ for every fixed $c$ (Kneser's satisfies this)
einfach: The super-logarithm counts how many times you have to take a logarithm. If you compare this for f(x) and for x, then in the limit exactly the number of exponential functions that are “hidden” in f remains: 0 for polynomials, 1 for 2^x or x^x, 2 for e^(e^x). With tetration there are also half-exponential functions — there the value is ½.

beweis.text:
(i) $A(e^y)=A(y)+1$; additivity via $A(f(g(x)))-A(x)=[A(f(g(x)))-A(g(x))]+[A(g(x))-A(x)]$; $A(T(A(x)+s))=A(x)+s$.
(ii) $A(x^2)-A(x)=A(\ln2+\ln\ln x)-A(\ln\ln x)\to0$ by hypothesis; $x^{\ln x}$ likewise one level deeper; $A(2^x)-A(x)=1+A(x\ln2)-A(x)\to1$.
Integrality for exp-log functions: Hardy (1910), for transseries: van der Hoeven (2006); there $\ln^{\circ n}\circ f\circ\exp^{\circ n}\sim\exp^{\circ k}$, hence $\chi=k$.
(iii) Because $\theta$ is periodic and uniformly continuous, $\theta(A(f))-\theta(A(x))$ vanishes for all choices if and only if $A(f)-A(x)$ tends to an integer.

formen.notiz: via iterated logarithms (practical for huge x)

titel: Ladder of levels: ln ln a is the m-th difference of ln H′ — for tetration, pentation, hexation, …
aussage:
(i) **Values:** $H_k(0)=1$, $H_k(1)=a$, $H_k(2)=H_{k-1}(a)$, and downward $H_k(-j)=-(j-1)$ for $j=1,\dots,k-3$:
$T(-1)=0$; $P(-1)=0$, $P(-2)=-1$; $H_6(-1)=0$, $H_6(-2)=-1$, $H_6(-3)=-2$. Each level inherits one more integer point.

(ii) **Slopes:** $H_{k+1}'(-j)/H_{k+1}'(-j-1)=H_k'(-j)$ for $0\le j\le k-3$, and from this for $m=0,1,2,\dots$
$$\ln\ln a=\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^j\binom{m}{j}\ln H_{3+m}'(-j).$$
$m=1$: $\ln a=T'(0)/T'(-1)$; $m=2$: $\ln a=\dfrac{P'(0)\,P'(-2)}{P'(-1)^2}$; $m=3$: $\ln a=\dfrac{H_6'(0)\,H_6'(-2)^3}{H_6'(-1)^3\,H_6'(-3)}$.
The individual slopes depend on the chosen solutions, these combinations do not. For $a=e$, $P'(0),P'(-1),P'(-2)$ form a geometric sequence
with ratio $T_e'(0)=1.0917673512\ldots$ (regular pentation at the fixed point: $1.08879$, $0.99727$, $0.91345$).
bereich: base $a>1$; $H_3(x)=a^x$, $H_{k+1}(x+1)=H_k(H_{k+1}(x))$, $H_{k+1}(0)=1$, every level strictly increasing and differentiable ($H_4=T$ tetration, $H_5=P$ pentation, $H_6$ hexation)
einfach: For tetration, ln a is the ratio of two slopes. One level higher, for pentation, you need three slopes, for hexation four — always with the signs and weights of a binomial row. Each level has one more integer point downward at which you know the value exactly.

beweis.text:
(i) $H_{k+1}(-1)=H_k^{-1}(1)=0$, because $H_k(0)=1$; inductively $H_{k+1}(-j-1)=H_k^{-1}(H_{k+1}(-j))=H_k^{-1}(-(j-1))=-j$, because $H_k(-j)=-(j-1)$.
(ii) Chain rule $H_{k+1}'(x+1)=H_k'(H_{k+1}(x))\,H_{k+1}'(x)$ at $x=-j-1$ with $H_{k+1}(-j-1)=-j$. With $\delta_k(j)=\ln H_k'(-j)$ this means
$\delta_{k+1}(j)-\delta_{k+1}(j+1)=\delta_k(j)$: the backward difference of a level is the level below. Applied $m$ times, one arrives at
$\delta_3(0)=\ln\bigl(\ln a\cdot a^0\bigr)=\ln\ln a$.

formen.notiz: Slopes of tetration as slope ratios of pentation
backward difference of a level = log. slope of the level below

aussage:
A **tetration to base $b$** is a function $F$ with
$F(x+1)=b^{F(x)}$ and $F(0)=1$, where $b^w:=e^{w\ln b}$ (principal branch of $\ln b$).
Without the normalization, $F$ is called a **superfunction** of $\exp_b$. Notation: $T_b$ for an
(arbitrary) solution, $T_b^{\mathrm K}$ for Kneser's solution.
bereich: $b>0,\ b\neq 1$; solution $F$ on an interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ or region $D\subset\mathbb C$ with $I+1\subset I$

aussage:
The analytic conjugacy class of a parabolic germ is determined by the transition maps
(horn maps) between the Fatou coordinates of adjacent petals. $f$ is the
time-one map of a holomorphic flow (formal iterates converge) if and only if these invariants are trivial.

aussage:
The tower converges if and only if there is a **unique** representation
$$b_1=t_1e^{-t_2},\quad b_2=t_2e^{-t_3},\ \dots,\ b_k=t_ke^{-t_1}\qquad\text{with}\quad|t_1t_2\cdots t_k|\le1$$
(Baker–Rippon 1989). For $k=2$ (bases $a,b$ alternating, $\varphi(x)=a^{b^x}$): convergence if and only if $\varphi$ has exactly one
fixed point $c$ with $|\varphi'(c)|\le1$, i.e. $\ln a=se^{-t}$, $\ln b=te^{-s}$ with unique $(s,t)$, $|st|\le1$ (Baker–Rippon 1985).
If all $b_n$ lie in $[-e,1/e]$, the tower converges even without periodicity (Barrow's theorem).

beweis.text: Baker–Rippon, Fibonacci Quart. 23 (1985) and Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 105 (1989), via the zbMATH reviews. The $t_j$ are the $b_j$-multiples of the points of the $k$-cycle, $t_1\cdots t_k$ is its multiplier.

titel: Below e^{−e} the phase becomes a square wave
aussage:
There is exactly one $x^*\in(0,1)$ with $T(x^*)=L$, and then $T(x^*+n)=L$ for all $n$ (the tetration **crosses the Julia set**).
$\Omega(x)=\lim_nT(x+2n)$ is a 2-periodic **square wave**: $z_A$ on $(x^*-1,x^*)$, $z_B$ on $(x^*,x^*+1)$ (mod 2), $\Omega(x^*)=L$.
There is no continuous 2-periodic limit function. Fourier: $c_0=\tfrac{z_A+z_B}2$, $c_k=\frac{i(z_A-z_B)e^{-i\pi kx^*}}{\pi k}$ for odd $k$,
0 for even ones. The shape is **universal**; only $x^*$ depends on the chosen tetration. Two rates: besides the jump $|\mu|^{n/2}$,
the width of the transition $|\lambda|^{-n}$ ($\lambda=cL<-1$).
bereich: $0<b<e^{-e}$, $T$ a continuous real tetration that crosses $L$ exactly once on $[0,1)$ (e.g. monotone on $[0,1]$)
einfach: Below e^(−e) the tower jumps between two values. If you draw the continuous tetration at even heights further and further up, its curve turns into a rectangle: at exactly one place it has to hit the repelling fixed point and gets stuck there.

beweis.text: $E$ is decreasing on ℝ, $E\circ E$ increasing with fixed points $z_B<L<z_A$; $(L,\infty)$ is the basin of $z_A$, $(0,L)$ of $z_B$, the only separating point is $L$. $T(0)=1>L>b=T(1)$ ⇒ intermediate value theorem. A continuous 2-periodic Ω would have a connected E-invariant image in two separate basins — impossible. Fourier series of the square wave.

gegenbeispielsuche: Original: three resp. four starting interpolations, |c_k|πk constant to 8 digits up to k = 41. exp.funde (linear starting interpolation, x* = 0.698330769): |c_k|πk = 0.7651944 … 0.7651888 for k = 1 … 41; T(x* + n) = L for n ≤ 12.

titel: Base change at a common fixed point is linear
aussage:
With $T_d(x)=\Psi_d(\lambda_d^{x}w_d)$ and $A_b=\log\sigma_b/\log\lambda_b$ one has, for $x\to-\infty$,
$$A_b\bigl(T_d(x)\bigr)=C_1+C_2\,x+\frac{a_1\,w_d}{\log\lambda_b}\,\lambda_d^{x}+O\bigl(\lambda_d^{2x}\bigr),\qquad
  C_2=\frac{\log\lambda_d}{\log\lambda_b},\quad C_1=\frac{\log w_d}{\log\lambda_b},$$
$a_1=\frac{u_d}{2(\lambda_d-1)}-\frac{u_b}{2(\lambda_b-1)}$. The deviation from the line decays like $|\lambda_d|^{x}$ — a
damped oscillation, **not a persistent periodic wave** as in the mixed-base phase law. If $b$ and $d$ have different
fixed points, $A_b(T_d(x))$ instead tends to a constant. The base change is exactly linear only for $b=d$.
bereich: two bases $b\ne d$ with a common fixed point $L$, $|\lambda_d|>1$, $|\lambda_b|\ne0,1$; $T_d$ regular at $L$ with $T_d(0)=1$, $A_b$ a regular Abel function at $L$
einfach: If you choose two bases that circle around the same point L and translate the height of one into the height of the other, a straight line C₁ + C₂·x comes out. The deviation from it shrinks with every step by the factor |λ| — no wave is left over. With different fixed points this does not work: then the translated height simply stays put.

beweis.text:
Both linearizations are normalized at the same point ($\sigma_b(L)=\Psi_d(0)-L=0$, derivative 1), so $h=\sigma_b\circ\Psi_d$ is tangent
to the identity: $h(v)=v+(p_{2,d}-p_{2,b})v^2+\dots$ with $p_2=u/(2(\lambda-1))$ (comparison of coefficients in $\Psi(\lambda w)=e^{u\Psi(w)}$).
Substituting $v=\lambda_d^xw_d\to0$ gives the formula. For different fixed points, $T_d(x)\to L_d\ne L$ and $A_b(T_d(x))\to A_b(L_d)$.
Exactly linear would mean $T_d(x)=T_b(C_1'+C_2x)$, hence $f_d=f_b^{\,C_2}$ in the regular iteration group; then $f_b,f_d$ commute:
$u_de^{u_bz}-u_be^{u_dz}\equiv$ const, differentiating gives $e^{u_bz}=e^{u_dz}$, hence $u_b=u_d$.

gegenbeispielsuche:
exp.gleiches_L, five pairs ($e^{\pi/2}$ with $e^{5\pi/2}$ and with $e^{-3\pi/2}$; $\sqrt2$ with $-\sqrt2$; $e$ with $e^{1-2\pi i/L_e}$; $2.084$ with $-1659.6$):
decay rate of the deviation = $\ln|\lambda_d|$ to 5 digits, first correction to $<4\cdot10^{-8}$ relative, best-fit line matches $C_2$ to $10^{-6}$.
Deviation at $x=-12$: $4\cdot10^{-12}$ … $2\cdot10^{-9}$; at $x=-1$ still 0.03 … 0.48 (linear only asymptotically).
Control test $e^{\pi/2}$ against $e$ (different L): slope $3.0\cdot10^{-3}$ at $x=-20$, $5.1\cdot10^{-6}$ at $x=-40$ (decays like $|L_e|^x$).

titel: Regular iteration at the complex fixed point L is not real
aussage:
Obvious approach: Koenigs function at $L$ (for $\log_b$, attracting) and $T:=\sigma^{-1}(\lambda^{x}c)$.
This gives a holomorphic superfunction that is **not real** on the real axis: $L$ and $\bar L$ are
on an equal footing, the choice of $L$ breaks the symmetry $T(\bar z)=\overline{T(z)}$.

beweis.text: For $|\lambda|>1$ one has $\lambda^{x}\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$, hence $F(x)=\sigma^{-1}(\lambda^x c)\to L\notin\mathbb R$. A function that is real on all of $\mathbb R$ cannot tend to $L$.

beweis.text: For $c<c'$: $T(x+c')\gg T(x+c)^N$, because $T(y+\delta)-T(y)\to\infty$; dominant monomial. Directly for every continuous strictly increasing solution: $m(\delta)=\min_{[0,1]}(T(y+\delta)-T(y))>0$ and $T(y+1+\delta)-T(y+1)\ge e^{T(y)}(e^{m}-1)$.

titel: Amplitude law from the imaginary period
aussage:
The Fourier coefficients of the difference $p=\alpha_A\circ\alpha_a^{-1}-\mathrm{id}$ decay like
$$|\hat p(k)|\approx C\,\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{2\pi^2 k}{|\ln\lambda_a|}\Bigr),$$
i.e. $p$ is holomorphic exactly in a strip of half the imaginary period $\pi/|\ln\lambda_a|$ of the regular tetration
at the lower fixed point. Heuristic: at $\operatorname{Im}\theta=\pi/|\ln\lambda_a|$, $\lambda_a^{\theta}$ turns by $\pi$,
$T^{\mathrm{reg}}$ reaches the other side of $a$, where $\alpha_A$ becomes singular.
